title: Brisk and the Missing Books
markdown:
The sun spilled over Ferncrown’s jagged peaks like a warm honey drop and painted the pine woods gold and emerald. Brisk the young goblin was already on his morning circuit, knapsack a little grubby, never without a few smooth stones or interesting leaves, bouncing against his knee. Pip rode his shoulder: a dusky-grey shadow, tiny squeaks like pebbles rolling down a mossy bank. Brisk loved those squeaks more than all the shiny pebbles in the woods.

“More pinecones?” he whispered, voice like rustling leaves. Pip answered with a flap and a little dance of agreement.

They were in their favourite stretch, where the air smelled of sweet pine sap and damp earth, and sunlight fell through tall straight trunks like golden coins on a green carpet. Brisk knew it as well as his own burrow. Safe. Familiar. A place that asked nothing of him except to notice.

He hummed a goblin tune. Then a sound drifted from further up the rocky path, faint as a whisper and twice as odd: a huffy-sputter-and-a-whirl. He paused. Head tilt. Bright robin-quick eyes narrowing. Pip stilled, ears twitching like tiny antennae.

“What’s that?” A tremble in the whisper. Knees like wobbly jelly. The prickle was new. He liked known paths. This sound had no name and no map. Curiosity tugged anyway, a kite-string at the heart.

The path steepened. Ground crunched under small boots. The air cooled and carried wild thyme and distant moss. They rounded a bend into a sun-drenched clearing, colourful pebbles, a very wobbly tower of spellbooks, and two people quite absorbed in their own weather.

The witch wore a tall pointed hat that seemed to defy gravity, dewdrop beads sparkling like miniature rainbows. Rings like trapped fireflies. She smelled of lavender and a little burnt sugar, a baking mishap that had decided to be pleasant. Her hands waved with great enthusiasm.

“But it’s my recipe for fizzy-pop potions,” she said, voice quick and high, a bubbling stream. “It clearly says three giggles and a sigh. You’ve put in a whole grumble. That will make them pop with a frown.”

The wizard’s silvery beard was practically a scarf and kept catching on spectacles perched precariously on his nose. He hummed a tuneless little tune and moved with slow thoughtful grace, a willow in a gentle breeze. Old parchment. Forgotten stories. Fresh rain.

“A grumble adds depth, Fizzwick dear,” he said, voice as gentle as falling snow. “It’s for my sleepy-time spells. It needs a touch of grumble. It helps the dreams settle in.”

They were arguing the way two playful squirrels chatter over a nut. Brisk’s heart thumped a tiny drum. Pip nudged his ear, a silent offer.

“But where’s the book?” Fizzwick wailed, dewdrop beads rattling. “My Fantastic Feasts and Fabulous Fancies is gone. I can’t find the moonbeam muffins without it. They’re simply not the same without a whisper of starlight.”

“And my Whispers from the Willow and Wanderings of the Wind has vanished,” sighed Glimmer, beard drooping. “I’m sure the dream-dust dumplings are in there. Fluffiest dumplings this side of the Whispering Woods.”

Brisk’s stomach did a flip-flop. The witch wrung her hands. The wizard tugged his beard. Neither noticed the small goblin or the bat. They looked like two large lost bumblebees who could not find the hive.

Then Brisk’s spotting-eyes found a small leather-bound book tucked beneath a particularly fluffy patch of moss near Glimmer’s foot. The sort of book that might hold muffins and dumplings. Cover worn from many readings. Peeking from under it, catching the light: a single familiar dewdrop bead.

Fizzwick sniffled. Glimmer looked as if he might try to knit a rainbow to cheer her. A firefly-spark of courage lit in Brisk. Deep breath. Little goblin chest out. Pip’s wings frantic against his ear. Tunic rough under his palm. Moss sweet and earthy underfoot.

“Excuse me,” he said, surprisingly clear, a small bell.

They stopped. Heads snapped up. Eyes like startled woodland creatures.

“Oh. Goodness me,” said Glimmer, fumbling his spectacles. “A young goblin. And a little flying friend. Well, hello there.”

“You startled me, little one,” chirped Fizzwick, wavy hands falling still. “We were just… having a moment.”

Brisk pointed a small green finger, hand trembling a little, voice steadier now. “That book. Under the moss. It looks rather like a recipe book.”

Glimmer bent slowly, beard a silvery river over pebbles, and lifted the moss. Leather embossed with constellations and swirling patterns.

“Why, bless my beard. It’s my book. Whispers from the Willow and Wanderings of the Wind. I was sure I’d lost it in the whirlwind of ideas.”

Fizzwick gasped. At the very edge, a tiny corner of faded floral cloth peeked out, little embroidered flowers. “My Fantastic Feasts and Fabulous Fancies. They must have been tucked together all along.”

Tension dissolved like morning mist. They looked at each other, at the two books, at Brisk. Glimmer’s smile crinkled his eyes. Fizzwick giggled a true bubbly giggle that made the dewdrop beads dance.

“Well, who could have guessed?” Glimmer chuckled, a warm rumble that filled the clearing.

“We were so busy grumbling and giggling we forgot to look properly,” Fizzwick added, clapping, beads tinkling. Kind curious eyes on Brisk. “Thank you, young goblin. You’ve saved our culinary creations and our peaceful afternoon.”

Warmth spread through him, not only the sun on his skin. He had spoken. He had pointed. He had helped. Pip squeaked happy and snuggled closer.

“You’re most welcome,” Brisk mumbled, a shy smile bigger and brighter than any pinecone he had ever collected.

Fizzwick and Glimmer, friends again, pored over the rediscovered books. Lavender, burnt sugar, old parchment, fresh rain, and the happy murmurs of feasts and dreamy spells. Brisk and Pip watched a moment, then turned down the rocky path. The woods felt friendlier. The sunlight warmer. The familiar path seemed to welcome them home. He would be back to the hidden terraces, perhaps not tomorrow, but soon. Next time the unknown would not feel quite so wobbly. He was Brisk, and he had been brave enough to say excuse me.
characters: Brisk (the young goblin), Pip (dusky-grey pet bat)
